title: The Small Sign Before the Big Sign
text:
In 1966 two Stanford psychologists, Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser, tested an old salesman's idea: get a foot in the door first. In one study, a researcher posing as a volunteer went door to door in Palo Alto, California, and asked homeowners to put a large, poorly lettered sign reading "Drive Carefully" on their front lawn. Shown a photo of the ugly sign, most people in the control group said no; only about one in six agreed.

Other homeowners had been visited two weeks earlier by a different volunteer with a tiny request: put a small, three-inch sign saying "Be a safe driver" in a window, or sign a petition. Almost everyone agreed to that. When those who had put up the small safe-driving sign later got the request for the big lawn sign, about three in four said yes; the other first requests raised agreement less, but still well above the control group.

The effect held even when the first request came from a different person and concerned a different issue, such as keeping California beautiful. Freedman and Fraser suggested that agreeing to the first request changed how people saw themselves: they had become the kind of person who supports good causes and helps when asked, and they acted to stay consistent with that picture.
lesson: Small commitments shape how we see ourselves, and that self-image drives bigger choices. Be careful which small requests you grant, and start small when you ask others for help.
source: Freedman, J. L., and Fraser, S. C. (1966). Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 4(2), 195-202.
